code.title: Mini test registry run by static initialisers

followUps:
Return a status value and make the macro propagate it, instead of throwing. Each assertion macro records the failure in the current test's result and, for ASSERT, does return from the enclosing function.

That is why ASSERT only works in functions returning void. The runner never sees an exception; it reads the result object after TestBody() comes back.

#define ASSERT_TRUE(c) \
  if (!(c)) { cur()->fail(#c); return; }

Cost is O(1) per assertion. Exceptions are optional and can be disabled with -fno-exceptions.

Because a function-local static is created the first time the function runs, so the registry always exists before the first test registers into it. A plain global vector in another file might not be constructed yet, since static-init order across files is unspecified (the "static initialisation order fiasco").

Example: 200 test files each push into registry() in an unknown order. Every call hits an already-built vector. Since C++11 the first-call initialisation is thread-safe, and the cost afterwards is one cheap flag check.

It runs the test binary with --gtest_list_tests, parses the Suite.Name lines, and creates one CTest entry per test that runs the binary with --gtest_filter=Suite.Name.

So ctest can run, retry, time and parallelise (-j8) tests individually, and show failures by name. With 300 tests you get 300 entries. Discovery happens at build time (POST_BUILD) or at ctest time (DISCOVERY_MODE PRE_TEST), so new tests appear without re-running CMake. The cost is one process launch per test.

code.title: ASSERT returns, EXPECT continues, fixture per test

followUps:
Because ASSERT does a bare return; and constructors and non-void functions cannot return that way, so the macro would not compile there (or would return nothing from a function that must return a value).

Also, a failed ASSERT in a constructor would leave a half-built object. Fixes: use EXPECT, put the check in a void helper called from the test body, or wrap the helper in ASSERT_NO_FATAL_FAILURE(helper());. Use SetUp() instead of the constructor when you need to ASSERT during setup, because SetUp returns void.

Run the tests in random order with several seeds, and run each test alone; any test that passes in one order and fails in another has a hidden dependency.

./tests --gtest_shuffle --gtest_random_seed=1234
./tests --gtest_filter=Suite.Name
./tests --gtest_repeat=50 --gtest_shuffle

Typical culprits are global or static state, files left in a temp directory, and singletons. Example: test B reads a counter that test A set to 5. B passes only after A, so a shuffle with 20 repeats exposes it quickly. Print the seed so a failure can be replayed.

code.title: Table-driven parameterised test with named cases

followUps:
Catch2's GENERATE runs the same test body once per generated value, and TEMPLATE_TEST_CASE runs it once per listed type.

TEST_CASE("port") {
  auto n = GENERATE(1, 80, 65535);
  REQUIRE(valid(n));
}
TEMPLATE_TEST_CASE("push", "", int, std::string) {
  Queue<TestType> q; q.push(TestType{});
}

Unlike GoogleTest there is no separate INSTANTIATE step: the table lives inside the test, and each value or type shows up as its own section in the report. 3 values give 3 runs.

Because fork() copies only the calling thread, so any mutex held by another thread at that moment stays locked forever in the child, which can deadlock it.

Example: a logging thread holds the allocator lock while the main thread forks; the child calls malloc and hangs. That is why death tests run first (suites named *DeathTest run before other tests) and use the "threadsafe" style, which re-executes the binary instead of forking: GTEST_FLAG_SET(death_test_style, "threadsafe"). The price is a full process start per test.

code.title: Stub, fake and mock behind an injected interface

followUps:
It picks the expectation that was declared last: GoogleMock searches expectations in reverse order of creation and uses the first one whose matchers all accept the call.

EXPECT_CALL(m, get(_)).WillRepeatedly(Return(0));
EXPECT_CALL(m, get(7)).WillOnce(Return(42));

Here get(7) returns 42 the first time, because the specific rule comes later. If the order were swapped, the catch-all would shadow it. So write general expectations first and specific ones after. Once a WillOnce is used up, further matching calls are errors (over-saturated) unless you add RetiresOnSaturation() to let older rules apply.

Put a seam around it: write your own small interface (an adapter) that wraps the third-party class, make production code depend on that interface, and mock the interface.

struct Clock { virtual ~Clock() = default; virtual long now() = 0; };
struct RealClock : Clock { long now() override { return ThirdParty::tick(); } };

Alternatives: make the code under test a template over the type (compile-time seam, no virtual cost), or use a link seam that substitutes a fake implementation at link time. Mocking a non-virtual method directly will not work, since nothing dispatches to the mock.

code.title: Redzones catch an off-by-one write

followUps:
ASan can miss bugs in code that was not compiled with it, memory errors that stay inside valid memory, and bugs on paths the tests never run.

Examples: a write that jumps over the 16-byte redzone into another valid object; a use-after-free after the quarantine has recycled the block (the quarantine is limited, for example 256 MB, so a long-delayed use can slip through); overflow within one struct (field A running into field B); uninitialised reads (that is MSan's job); and data races (TSan). Running with a larger redzone (ASAN_OPTIONS=redzone=64) and detect_stack_use_after_return helps a little.

Because MSan tracks "is this bit initialised" through every copy and calculation, and a function that was not instrumented writes memory without updating that tracking, so MSan thinks the data is uninitialised and reports false errors.

Example: read(fd, buf, 10) inside an uninstrumented libc fills buf, but MSan's shadow still says "uninitialised"; the next if (buf[0]) then gets reported. So you rebuild libc++ and all dependencies with -fsanitize=memory (or add interceptors for system calls). That setup cost is why MSan is mostly run in a nightly job.

code.title: Vector clocks: race vs happens-before

followUps:
Because TSan uses happens-before: it reports two unsynchronised accesses even if the bad interleaving never occurred in this run.

Plain locks and atomics tell TSan about ordering through its instrumented calls. A custom lock-free queue built from raw atomics usually works as is. Where it does not (inline asm, an uninstrumented library), tell TSan with annotations:

ANNOTATE_HAPPENS_BEFORE(&slot);   // producer, after publishing
ANNOTATE_HAPPENS_AFTER(&slot);    // consumer, after reading

Better is to use std::atomic with release/acquire, which TSan understands with no annotation.

Because x86 being strongly ordered does not stop the compiler: without an atomic, the compiler may keep the flag in a register, hoist the read out of a loop, or reorder code around it, and it is also undefined behaviour in C++.

bool done = false;                 // bug
while (!done) {}                   // can compile to an infinite loop
// fix: std::atomic<bool> done{false};

Also, data written before setting the flag may not be visible to the reader without release/acquire. It may work in tests and break with -O2 or on ARM.

code.title: Warning ratchet: fail only on new warnings

followUps:
GCC computes some warnings from optimiser information such as inlining, value ranges and flow analysis, and those passes only run when optimisation is on.

Examples: -Wmaybe-uninitialized, -Wnull-dereference, -Wstringop-overflow and -Warray-bounds need the inlined code and known value ranges. At -O0 nothing is inlined, so the compiler cannot prove the bad path. So CI must build at least once with -O2 and the same flags as release, otherwise the 4 000 warnings count is incomplete, and fixing at -O0 hides some of them.

Treat them as code you do not own: mark them as system headers so their warnings are not shown, and keep your own warnings strict.

target_include_directories(app SYSTEM PRIVATE third_party/include)
# or on the command line: -isystem third_party/include

With -isystem, GCC and Clang suppress most warnings from those headers. Do the same for clang-tidy with HeaderFilterRegex limited to your own directories. Do not edit vendored code; if a real bug appears, report it upstream or patch it in a tracked patch file.

code.title: Coverage-guided fuzzing finds a magic prefix

followUps:
Wrap the API in a fuzz harness that turns the input bytes into a sequence of operations: each byte or group of bytes picks an operation and its arguments.

for (size_t i = 0; i + 1 < size; i += 2) {
  switch (data[i] % 3) {
    case 0: s.push(data[i+1]); break;
    case 1: s.pop(); break;
    case 2: s.clear(); break;
  }
}

Check invariants after each step, or compare with a simple reference model (differential testing). Or use FuzzedDataProvider to read typed values. Input of 100 bytes gives about 50 calls, and the fuzzer's coverage feedback finds the call sequences that matter.

Usually a timeout means an algorithmic bug (accidental quadratic or exponential work, or an endless loop) and an OOM means unbounded allocation driven by an attacker-controlled size field.

Example: a 12-byte input says "2 billion items follow" and the parser calls reserve(2000000000) before checking. Fix by validating sizes against the remaining input and putting a limit on work. They matter for security because they are denial-of-service. Use -timeout=5 and -rss_limit_mb=2048 so they are reported as findings instead of hanging the run.

code.title: MC/DC independence pairs for (a && b) || c

followUps:
Because compilers generate a separate copy of code for each template instance and each macro expansion, so one source line can map to many counters, and gcov may show a line as covered when only some instances ran.

Example: max<int> and max<string> are two functions; if only the int one runs, a line may look 100% covered while the other copy is untested. Macros expand at the call site, so one macro line has many branches that all map to one line number. gcovr and llvm-cov can show per-instantiation views. Check the instantiation report rather than trusting the line total.

Find, for each condition, two test rows that differ only in that condition and give different results. N conditions need at least N+1 tests, here 4.

Rows (a,b,c) and result:

  • a: TFF=F and TTF=T (b true, c false)
  • b: FTF=F and TTF=T
  • c: FTF=F and FTT=T (a false)

The set {TTF, FTF, TFF, FTT} covers all three pairs. Branch coverage alone would be satisfied by only 2 tests (TTF gives true, FFF gives false), so MC/DC is stricter.

code.title: Benchmark with DoNotOptimize and median of repetitions

followUps:
Because timing results have occasional large spikes (a context switch, a page fault, a frequency change) and the median ignores them, while the mean is dragged up by a single bad run.

Example: 9 runs take 100 us and one takes 900 us. The mean is 180 us, which no run actually resembled. The median is 100 us. The mean is still useful for throughput totals, but for comparing two implementations use the median together with the spread (for example the coefficient of variation) over 20 or more repetitions.

Run the benchmarks in CI on a dedicated, quiet machine, save results as JSON, and compare each commit with a stored baseline, flagging changes bigger than the normal noise.

./bench --benchmark_format=json --benchmark_out=new.json
compare.py benchmarks base.json new.json

Fail or alert when the median is, say, more than 5 percent worse with a significant p-value (compare.py gives a Mann-Whitney U test). Keep a time series (a dashboard) so slow drift of 1 percent per week is visible. Run noisy shared CI runners only for coarse alerts.

A core file holds the process's memory (stack, heap and data mappings) and the registers of every thread at the crash, but not the program's code or symbols, and not files or the state of other processes.

So you need the exact binary and its debug info with the same build-id to read it. It does not contain open file contents, network peers, or memory that was excluded (marked MADV_DONTDUMP, or cut by ulimit -c). It can contain secrets (keys, passwords) from memory, so treat it as sensitive data. A full core can be many GB for a big service.

A minidump is a small file (often under a few MB) with the thread stacks, registers, loaded module list and some memory near the crash, while a full core has the whole address space.

Crashpad can write minidumps on the user's machine and upload them, since a 30 GB core is not practical. You lose heap contents unless they are included, so you debug with stack traces and symbol files (.sym from the build). A minidump is enough for most crashes at the top of stacks; a corruption bug may still need a full core or a local reproduction.

Run only what changed and run it in parallel: cache builds, split the test suite, and move slow work to nightly jobs.

Use ccache or sccache (a cache hit cuts a 10 minute build to about 1 minute), build only the targets affected by the diff, shard ctest across runners (ctest -j plus 4 shards turns 20 minutes into about 5), run clang-tidy only on changed files, and cancel older runs when new commits arrive. Set a time budget (15 minutes) and treat going over it as a bug. Heavy items (MSan, long fuzzing, full tidy) stay in the nightly pipeline.

Install the library to a temporary prefix, then build a tiny separate consumer project that calls find_package(MyLib REQUIRED) against that prefix and links the imported target.

cmake --install build --prefix /tmp/stage
cmake -S test/consumer -B cbuild -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/tmp/stage
cmake --build cbuild && ctest --test-dir cbuild

This catches missing headers, wrong include paths, missing exported targets and unset version files. Run it in the matrix for static and shared builds. If it only works when run from the source tree, the package is broken for users.

Measure it with mutation testing: if tests really check behaviour, small deliberate bugs in the code should make them fail.

A tool like Mull changes the code (for example < to <=, + to -) and reruns the tests. Example: 100 mutants, tests kill 60, so the mutation score is 60 percent. High line coverage with a low score means tests run code without checking it. Also check review signals: do expected values come from a spec rather than copied from the code, do the tests fail on a known-bad version, and how many flaky tests appear.

Only under strict conditions: the fixes must be mechanical, small, reviewed, and proved by tests, and never applied blind across the whole codebase.

Safe examples are modernize-use-override or readability-* fixes, applied in a separate PR with the full test and sanitizer run. Risky ones are fixes that change behaviour (such as performance-move-const-arg or bugprone fixes), where a human must read the diff. Conditions: a clean baseline before, one check per PR, CI green including sanitizers, the agent cannot add NOLINT or disable checks, and a person approves the merge.
